newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Taleban battle foes amid talk of peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Taleban battle foes amid talk of peace deal.

text.p: Fighting raged between the Taleban and their foes north of Kabul on Thursday amid talk of a Pakistani-brokered peace deal between the purist Islamic militia and an opposition force in northern Afghanistan.

Taleban jets bombed positions held by opposition guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood as heavy fighting continued around the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of the Afghan capital, a Pakistan-based news service said. The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted Taleban sources as saying the militia controlled parts of the town, including an army barracks and cement factory, while Masood held other parts.
Jabal os-Siraj controls access to the Salang highway which leads to the north over the towering Hindu Kush mountains.

The Taleban sources said a barrage of artillery and rocket fire had forced them to withdraw from the nearby town of Golbahar, the gateway to Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold, on Wednesday after suffering undisclosed casualties.

North of the Hindu Kush, a stranded Taleban force led by Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said it had beaten back an attack by ethnic Uzbek opposition troops on its positions at Robatak, 30 km (19 miles) northwest of Pul-i-Khumri. AIP quoted Taleban sources as saying 70 opposition fighters had been killed and 30 captured in the battle for the hilly area, but gave no figures for Taleban casualties. No independent account of the fighting was available.

In Islamabad, a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman said the Taleban had accepted peace proposals made by Uzbek opposition leader General Abdul Malik, who handed the Islamic militia a stinging defeat in the north last week.
But a Taleban official, Wakil Ahmad, would not confirm that Malik's terms had been accepted and demanded the release of Taleban prisoners held in the northern capital Mazar-i-Sharif.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said in a statement on Thursday that it was preparing to register about 700 prisoners held in Mazar-i-Sharif after last week's fighting.
Among Malik's captives are the Taleban foreign minister, Mullah Mohammad Ghous, northern commander Mullah Abdul Razzak and central bank chief Mullah Ahsanullah.
"Our condition for talks is that they must release our prisoners," Ahmad told AIP, but stopped short of saying that no negotiations could take place before the prisoners were freed.
"I cannot reject the possibility of talks," he said.
The Pakistani spokesman said earlier that Malik had set three conditions for a peace deal, which he had passed to the Pakistani consul-general in Mazar-i-Sharif.

Malik had demanded that the Taleban let northern groups keep "exclusive control" of the north, stop trying to disarm opposition fighters there and agree to an "Islamic dispensation" that Malik would set up in cooperation with the Taleban.
"This message was conveyed to the Taleban shura (council) and (its Kandahar-based chief) Mullah Mohammad Omar and they agreed to all these basic principles," the spokesman said.
Pakistan conveyed the Taleban response to Malik on Saturday, the spokesman said, adding: "A reply is expected any time."
Asked if he could confirm that Malik's proposals had been accepted, Ahmad, who is based in Kandahar, said: "It is possible that we will accept some points." He declined to elaborate.
It was not clear if Malik had consulted Masood or other opposition leaders before making his peace overture.

Any Taleban agreement to Malik's proposals would mark a drastic policy change for the Islamic militia, which has hitherto shown implacable determination to force all opposition factions to bend to its will and surrender.

Malik defected to the Taleban last month in a mutiny against former opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, but switched sides again after Taleban fighters entered Mazar-i-Sharif and began enforcing their strict Islamic code.
Malik's Uzbek troops linked up with Shi'ite Moslem militiamen to drive the Taleban out of the city in street battles that cost the Taleban an estimated 300 dead.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul in September, are trying to impose strict Islamic rule throughout war-ravaged Afghanistan.
